newsitem.title: USA: IBM in global electronic commerce deal.
newsitem.headline: IBM in global electronic commerce deal.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp.'s new Internet Division unveiled a worldwide alliance Tuesday aimed at promoting electronic commerce.

The new alliance, called CommercePOINT Partnership, complements a suite of products the computer giant announced last week by providing a common forum in which companies can conduct business and exchange ideas.
IBM also has joined with Washington, D.C.-based Universal Business Exchange, or UNIBEX, to expand CommercePOINT to international markets.
More than half a dozen major organisations have joined the project, they said.

"The technology for electronic transactions has been there all along, what's been missing is the service," John Kalb, vice president of electronic commerce at IBM, told Reuters following a news conference here.

Kalb conceded that as recently as this past spring, companies were expressing concerns about conducting secure electronic transactions. In the past six months, however, vast improvements in sharing secure technology have been made.
The result has been that businesses are now asking for services like CommercePOINT to help usher in a new age of electronic commerce, Kalb said.

Mady Jalinous, chairman of UNIBEX, which has previously been known as the IBEX Global Business Alliance, said the new system would assist in electronically matching parties in different parts of the world.

Jalinous said the alliance with IBM would aim to "expand our vision of what is electronic commerce" by making it easier for organisations using different languages and different customs to communicate and trade.
In many ways, the network aims to create new marketplaces where cultural and geographical barriers have created inefficiencies, Jalinous told Reuters in an interview.
Key to the effort, Jalinous said, is the ability to issue and administer electronic signatures on a global basis, with IBM providing the technology and UNIBEX the administration.
UNIBEX plans to offer services ranging from market research and mass-marketing to generating qualified leads and purchase order invoices, he said.

Jalinous said the goal was to offer businesses in Djakarta and Seattle, for example, the ability to engage in commerce with no additional costs or risks compared with established business partnerships at closer range.

The services will take advantage of IBM's global computing network as well as, eventually, the Internet, enabling users to "point and click their way" between internal corporate networks, or Intranets, and the public domain.
Other members of the alliance are the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, accountancy firm Deloitte & Touche, AT&T Corp., Dun and Bradstreet, Simon & Shuster, and Chase Manhattan Bank.

One small provider of security for electronic transactions, Austin, Texas-based TradeWave Corp., claims CommercePOINT will help bring trust to his market and agility in providing customised products to its customers.
"As a small businessman, I am bullish around CommercePOINT," said Roy Smith, heads of TradeWave.
The participants will contribute content, services, distribution channels and technology, according to Colby Mims, special projects manager at IBM's Internet unit.
Jalinous said he expects 35,000 subscribers in 1997 and that even by conservative estimates, he projects 1.8 million in the fifth year.

Small and medium-size enterprises might pay $1,500 to $4,000 for the service, while larger firms could pay tens of thousands of dollars, he added. Jalinous expects to raise additional funds with a public stock offering, possibly in 1997.
